utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Trbojevic, good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Ackerman will arrive after the break. We have with us our assistant, Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a couple of first of all. I've given to the Defence this morning, and I hope Your Honours -- no it's going to be handed to Your Honours now, I think, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't received any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall that I spent sometime yesterday asking -- are we in open session? Yes, we are -- the witness about a meeting in Doboj, and you will recall that he had some difficulty in remembering who was there. After court yesterday, I made some inquiries as to whether we had any other documents within the system that might assist. And, Your Honours, what it produced was these: A newspaper article from a newspaper which I may say I've not heard of before, called Derventski List, I think it's published in the municipality of Derventa. And it's dated the 13th of February and says last weekend but by a process of elimination and by the consent, one can see it's referring to that meeting. Should there be any doubt, we also found -- and this comes from the Derventski List is open source material; in other words, it's a newspaper. The second document came from the Banja Luka collection, which was disclosed in its entirety to the Defence on CD-ROM and some considerable, almost years ago now, I think, but it's not one that we've actually formally produced before. But, Your Honours, I would wish to use them this morning with the witness just to see if he can refresh his memory from this, unless there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection on your part, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the first thing. Your Honour, the second one relates to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Permission granted, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It relates to the order of witnesses, which I'm afraid we've been changing over and over again, really at the request of the Defence because they don't want major witnesses together. But you will recall yesterday, when I dealt with Witness 7.45, the gentleman who is going to be testifying for the fifth time, Mr. Ackerman said that he was going to be spending some five days in cross-examination of him. Well, Your Honour, it may be I'll have something to say about that at the stage when we get to. But the fact is even if that's overemphasising or exaggerating how long it will take, we couldn't complete him in Monday and Tuesday of next week. I shall be short in chief, because as I say everything is covered in the Stakic transcript. So -- and what happened when he testified in Stakic was that he had to go away and come back again because there was a break. I think that's highly undesirable. So we are not going to call him next week. I told Mr. Ackerman about that yesterday afternoon, and he was content with that. I said we were going it try and replace him with a much shorter witness, and again he told me that he didn't have any objection, provided there weren't a great many transcripts. We are attempting to get hold of a short witness, who has only testified once before or possibly not at all. There are a few who have never testified. We are waiting this morning for confirmation who that witness will be and we'll inform the Defence as soon as we know, and Your Honours. If we can't, it may be that we'll have a problem on Monday and Tuesday filling -- using the time for any witnesses but that probably won't upset the Defence too much because it will give them extra time. Your Honour, the second matter goes back to the question of the transcripts, and this really is because it's an administrative nightmare to copy the huge numbers of transcripts and exhibits and whatever, and not to mention the expense. Yesterday -- no, Monday, I raised with Your Honours the problem that I was foreseeing with the agreement made with Mr. Ackerman that it hadn't been our intention - and it's my fault for not making the wording clearer - to rely on every single transcript merely the one that covered where a witness, like 7.45, had testified so often. The one that covered all the areas, and in his case, that's his Stakic testimony. Your Honours, I think were going to rule on the application and I've been asked by those who have the dealings with this copying whether Your Honours would make a ruling one way or another because if all we are relying on is the transcript, for example, in Stakic, then it only means copying that transcript for everybody. And if Mr. Ackerman wants to cross-examine or make the other transcripts, then of course we are do the copying necessary, but at the moment we are copying everything in advance. So that's the situation. I see Mr. Ackerman is going to be coming later so it may be -- if that could be passed on to him in the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, Ms. Korner, the position is very -- is a very simple one. We would only be interested in having a copy of the transcript that you're going to make use of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well in that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest we don't need, unless we are specifically referred to those other transcripts, either the way Mr. Ackerman himself suggested yesterday, which frankly, if you ask me, could happen in one or two instances but not necessarily in the case of each and every witness who has testified before. Unless we are -- we need to refer to those other transcripts, we don't need them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I thought, Your Honour. It seems to me eminently sensible that unless they are brought in in some way or other, what we rely on we will make an exhibit and provide to Your Honours. And if other transcripts are brought in, then we will make the appropriate copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is also the problem of space in our chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because with Hadzihasanovic, with Mrksic, as one of the permanent judges in Trial Chamber II, I receive all the documentation coming in during the pre-trial stage of the other cases. So I have folders and folders and folders cropping up from everywhere. You know, it's becoming impossible. So this already -- this case is already impossible with the huge amount of documentation. So the less documents -- I would have preferred in fact, were it not for the fact that we need them here, to have everything on CD-ROM. It's much easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I know that -- this is slightly off the point, but I know there are discussions going on at the moment between the various parties to these trials as to trying to produce some sort of electronic format for all these documents and statements and the like. And it's clear -- this trial I think has shown because it's the first really major document trial to have taken place exactly how onerous it can be. But, Your Honour, in that case that's what we will do, and I'm grateful to Your Honour force that indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we now go into closed session and bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I told that I did my response to the judicial notice motion and it's filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Although it says the date on it is in January. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect that the correct date will be put on it by somebody. The other motion that I need to deal with is -- it's a motion of 21 October dealing with Rule 92 bis Prijedor. It's quite a long motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm meeting actually one of my legal assistants immediately after the sitting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was working on it a bit yesterday afternoon and this morning, and what I would like Your Honours to allow me to do - and I'll explain why - is to facilitate matters to reply basically witness by witness rather than wait until I've completed all the work I have to do to reply, and here is why: If I take the first one, 7.138, it is alleged that he fits under Rule 92 because his testimony will only corroborate that of Witness 7.78, 7.226, 7.225, 7.46, 7.3, 7.134. That means in order to just answer with that -- with regard to that one witness, I need to read the transcripts of those others. Now, some I have read, some I have not. And what I tell you -- I will tell you is that I will work through this as rapidly as I possibly can, but it's your order that I must file a reasoned objection if I'm going to object to being Rule 92. To do that, I have to do this kind of preparation. And if there is a better way, that Your Honours suggest for me to respond to, I would be happy to do it. But that seems to me in terms of just how to move through it, efficiently and rapidly, that would be the way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I take it from what Madam Richterova said during the formal meeting that we had in my chambers that tomorrow morning we are to expect a revised list --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Order, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I would -- first, let me give you the floor to respond to what Mr. Ackerman said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think there is -- I don't think we have any strong feelings about it in the sense that although we hoped to complete the Prijedor part before Christmas, it clearly is going to go on beyond Christmas, though I hope not by much. All I can say is this: That none of these selected witnesses give any direct testimony against Mr. Brdjanin. If that had been the case, we would have called them. For example, the witness that he's just picked on, 7.138, is someone who was in Keraterm and that's -- he's just supporting what is effectively, I don't think, argued any longer that Keraterm was a deeply unpleasant place. But as far as we are concerned, unless Mr. Ackerman thinks it is likely that any of these crime-base witnesses will be required to be brought here for cross-examination, which is effectively what we are doing with most of the witnesses, effectively they are transcripts plus cross, then we don't mind one way or the other when he gets through it. But I think it's mainly those that we will have to notify that they are required to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, there are some already, Your Honour, that I'm absolutely going to request attend and I already know why, but I want to do the rest of the reading just so that I can give you a reasoned thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I said, I have someone going through the motion and preparing a memo. I personally am not exactly familiar with the details of the motion as yet. I will be discussing it first time with my legal assistant soon after this sitting. And I suppose I should be in the position to form an opinion pretty soon, probably by tomorrow, and then we'll see. We could also perhaps, if there are -- if there are some witnesses about whom your position -- you already know what position you're going to take, then perhaps we can do it in stages. You can file, without further delay, a response with regard to -- a reply with regard to those witnesses and there will be, of course, time to file further response with regard to the others. We could do it that way as well. But I myself am not exactly familiar with the details yet. I still have to go through the list and see what's cooking there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you just suggested is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can work it out that way. Where you know you're not going to object or where you know that you are going to just ask for the presence of the witness for cross-examination purposes, I think there is no reason why you should delay filing a reply. Where there is reason for such a delay because you need to go deeper into the matter and read transcripts, then obviously, I mean, the Chamber is not going to tell you no. All right. So we will resume tomorrow morning, 9.00 in this same hall. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.49 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of November, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 25
